target_customer: Quick-service restaurant franchisees and chains that run drive-thrus and dining rooms
problem: Fast food owners could not reliably measure speed of service. Hellometer uses cameras and computer vision to time each car and guest and show where slowdowns occur.
business_model: B2B SaaS per location, with camera hardware
product_category: Computer vision operations analytics for restaurants

founders.name: Alexander Popper
prior_employers: Google (led privacy engineering efforts, per Hellometer press release naming CEO Alex)
founders.background_notes: YC page lists only him and gives no bio. The Intel partnership release gives the first name Alex only; the surname link comes from the YC page.

founders.name: Alberto Rivera
prior_employers: Ford Autonomous Vehicles research group (computer vision AI, per Hellometer release naming CTO Alberto)
founders.background_notes: Surname and co-founder status come from a third party company overview seen in search results; the release itself does not use the word founder.

competitors.name: HME ZOOM Nitro
competitors.what: In-ground loop and sensor based drive-thru timers with a dashboard
competitors.traction_then: Established product line; a Taco Bell operator reported a 60 second gain after install (undated NRN item)
competitors.funding_then: HME is a long-established hardware company

technical_complexity.rationale: Camera based vehicle and guest tracking from ordinary security cameras across varied sites, which needed reliable computer vision with a two person team.

defensibility.rationale: Camera timers can be copied by well-funded vendors. Installed hardware and data per store create some switching cost.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Incumbent timer vendors added vision based timers later (DTiQ Vision Timer, Berry AI entered); none acquired Hellometer as far as found.

market_need_then: The company states that every 7 seconds of service improvement lifts same-store revenue about 1%, and that owners had no reliable measurement. A QSR trade study reported timer stores were about 30 seconds faster.

branding.domain_note: Moved from hellometer.io to hellometer.ai (301 redirect seen in 2026).

identity.voice_and_tone: Plain operational language aimed at restaurant owners: 'Making fast food faster'.

branding.community_and_virality: No community or merch evidence found. Trade press covered a 2023 Intel partnership.

brand_strength.rationale: Customer logos such as Subway and Carl's Jr. appear on its site and trade press ran the Intel release, but no brand-level coverage exists.

outcome_analysis: Hellometer remains an operating company with a small team. It expanded from drive-thru timers to lobby timers, loss prevention and kitchen monitoring and lists customers including Subway, Carl's Jr. and Church's Chicken. Funding is not publicly verified, so growth is judged only from product breadth and a 2023 Intel partnership.
notes: CB Insights shows $1.13M total and Standout shows a $250K seed; both are aggregators and conflict, so no round is recorded. QSR Magazine pages returned 403 and are not cited. No acquisition, shutdown or layoff news found. Berry AI and DTiQ Vision Timer appear in later search results, so they are excluded from founding competition. Completeness pass: Round recorded rests on a single database, CB Insights (Seed II, $1M, 2024-10-10; total $1.13M over 5 rounds); Standout ($250K seed) and geo.sig.ai ($150K from 8 investors) conflict; earlier rounds not itemized.
